column4: The garden-dweller recalls his companion mocking him for affirming resurrection; this supplies the personal act of denial behind the section's companion, fall, and fire meeting.
The saved man looks down and sees his former companion in the midst of Hell, directly joining height, downward sight, and the fire below.
He tells the companion that he nearly brought him to ruin, making another person's pull toward a fall part of the fire scene.
The speaker attributes his absence from Hell solely to his Lord's favor, which sharpens the section's distinction between an unrepaid human favor and the saving divine favor.
God's favor makes former enemies brothers and rescues them from the brink of a pit of fire; brink, rescue, favor, and guidance occupy one scene exactly as the section describes.
Moses and Aaron are taught to tell Pharaoh that peace belongs to the one who follows guidance, opening the palace encounter with the section's offered path.
Their message assigns punishment to whoever denies and turns away, bringing the two acts of 92:16 into the same confrontation with Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron who their Lord is; the question stages the contest between the king who claims lordship and the Lord who gives.
Moses answers that their Lord gave every thing its created form and then guided it, joining creation, giving, and guidance in the single divine action highlighted by the section.
Pharaoh proclaims himself the highest lord, a direct usurpation of the title belonging to the Lord Most High whose face the giver seeks.
God seizes Pharaoh with the punishment of the latter and the former, answering his claim of supremacy with God's ownership of the last and the first.

The ayah denies that righteousness is merely turning faces, then defines it through giving loved wealth, freeing necks, truthfulness, and taqwa; it is the section's face, hand, release, affirmation, and shield in one definition.
The feeders say they feed only for God's face and want neither repayment nor thanks, directly joining the giving hand, the sought face, and refusal of human return.
Their fear of a grim, frowning Day supplies the protective fear behind their unrecompensed giving and makes the threatened day itself wear a face.
God shields them from that Day's evil and grants radiance and joy, completing the section's movement from fearful face and protective giving to an opened face.
A person vows that if God gives from His bounty, he will certainly give charity and be righteous, tying divine giving to the human promise to give.
Spending for God's approval is a garden on high ground whose rain yields double produce, directly uniting giving, sought approval, height, rain, and growth.
A building founded on taqwa and God's approval is set against one on a collapsing cliff-edge that falls with its builder into Hell, the section's shielded height and fiery abyss in one comparison.
Hoarded treasure is heated in Hell and brands foreheads, flanks, and backs, making wealth cling as fire to the very face, side, and turned back of its keeper.
Moses sees a fire during the night and hopes to find guidance at it, directly presenting the fire read from a safe distance as a sign along the road.
Moses tells his family that the fire may yield news or a burning brand so they can warm themselves; its form of the ṣ-l-y root makes nearness to fire warming here where entering Hell burns.
Spending is to be done only in seeking God's face, and whatever is spent is repaid in full; this directly clarifies the section's giving for the face without seeking repayment from recipients.
Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and openly, join the surah's opening times to its giving hand and receive their reward from their Lord.
Giving the due of kin, the needy, and the traveler is declared good for those who desire God's face, joining directed wealth and the sought face.
Riba given to grow within people's wealth does not grow with God, while zakat given seeking His face makes its givers the multipliers; it joins face, giving, purification, and true increase.
Those seeking their Lord's face persist, pray, spend secretly and openly, and repel evil with good, placing the face sought and the giving act within one steadfast course.
Righteousness cannot be attained until one spends from what one loves, concentrating the same bond between loved wealth and true goodness that 2:177 supplies to the section.
The claim that God's hand is fettered is reversed by the declaration that His hands are outspread and He spends as He wills, directly opposing the clenched hand to the giving Lord.
The command pictures a hand chained to the neck or spread without limit, giving the section's held and opened hands a bodily measure rather than treating either posture abstractly.
Those summoned to spend include one who is stingy only against himself; God is self-sufficient while humans are needy, directly reversing the miser's claim to independence.
Those who are stingy and command stinginess are warned that whoever turns away cannot diminish God, the self-sufficient and praiseworthy, joining withholding, turning, and true independence.
Fear God, listen, obey, and spend; whoever is protected from the avarice of the self prospers, so giving, taqwa, and a protective barrier against inner stinginess stand together.

What people withhold from God's bounty will be collared around their necks, while the inheritance of heaven and earth belongs to God; gripped wealth becomes its owner's grip and divine ownership remains.
God shows the human being the two elevated ways, a particularly close counterpart to the section's road dividing before its walkers.
The person nevertheless does not undertake the steep ascent, turning the moral choice into the section's concrete contrast of height and descent.
The steep ascent is defined first as freeing a neck, meeting the section's use of 2:177 to place release in the giving hand.
Feeding on a day of severe hunger makes the difficult upward road an act of provision rather than an image of height alone.
The orphan of near relation identifies one recipient of the feeding by which the steep way is climbed.
The destitute person in misery identifies the low human condition toward which the giver's hand reaches.
Faith, mutual patience, and mutual mercy make such givers companions of the right, completing the section's road according to the character of its walkers.
Those who climb through faith and giving are named companions of the right, turning the split path into a final side.
Faces on that Day are radiant, matching the section's face disclosed after darkness and protected from the frowning Day.
Those faces are pleased with their striving, directly joining the surah's diverse striving to its final رضى.
They are in a lofty garden, bringing pleased striving, the opened face, height, and garden into the same sequence.
The condemned person says his wealth did not avail him, voicing from inside judgment exactly what the section says the falling miser discovers.
He says his authority has vanished, pairing failed wealth with the loss of claimed power like the king brought down from supremacy.
The command to seize and shackle him replaces the hand that grasped wealth with a stronger hand taking hold of him.
The next command sends the seized man into Hell, completing the movement from useless wealth and fallen authority to entry into fire.
The threatened blaze is named immediately before the acts that summon its victim, grounding the following turned back and hoarded wealth in fire rather than in a generic rebuke.
The blaze strips away the skin, a bodily counterpart to the treasure heated against faces, sides, and backs in the section.
The fire calls the person who turned his back and went away, directly joining fire to the bodily turn of refusal.
That person gathered and withheld, so hoarded wealth and the back turned to warning form one character exactly as in the section.
A condemned man's wealth and earnings do not avail him, a terse parallel to wealth failing at the instant of ruin.
He will enter a flaming fire, placing that failed wealth directly beside the act of entering the blaze.
On the judgment day neither wealth nor children benefit, establishing the boundary at which possession ceases to be a saving hand.
The audience is asked to consider the fire it kindles, shifting attention from Hell alone to an actual humanly approached fire.
God asks whether humans made its tree or He did, returning even the usable fire to the Lord who creates and gives each thing its capacity.
God made that fire a reminder and a provision for travelers, almost exactly the section's fire serving as warning-sign and help on a night road.
Moses sees a fire after completing his term and tells his family he may bring news or a brand so they may warm themselves, a full parallel to the guiding night-fire.
When Moses reaches the fire he is called from the blessed spot, showing that the approached sign carries a divine voice rather than consuming him.
On reaching the fire Moses hears a blessing upon those at and around it and God's transcendence proclaimed, continuing the fire-as-revelatory-sign scene.
When Moses reaches the fire he is called by name, supplying the voice at the end of the night approach anticipated in 20:10.
At the fire God says the Hour is coming and partly concealed so that every soul is repaid for what it strives, joining hiddenness, striving, and repayment.
Moses is warned not to let one who denies the Hour and follows desire turn him from it and bring him to ruin, echoing the companion who nearly ruins the believer.
God declares that the direction of the path rests upon Him while some paths deviate, a close formulation of divine guidance amid the section's forked road.
God's straight path is to be followed rather than the several paths that divide their walkers, making the section's diverging courses an explicit command.
The human being is asked from what God created him, opening a creation-and-road sequence parallel to the section's palace answer.
God creates the human from a drop and measures him, giving created form and measure before the way is eased.
God then eases the way for the human, a direct counterpart to the two ways made easy according to the walker.
The command to glorify the name of the Lord Most High restores the title Pharaoh claimed to its proper bearer and matches the face of the Lord Most High sought by the giver.
The Most High creates and proportions, restating the first half of Moses' account of the Lord in the palace.
He determines and then guides, bringing measure and guidance together just as the section's giver-Creator makes the road fit.
The Hereafter and the first life belong to God, nearly restating the ownership claim by which the section brings down Pharaoh's supremacy.
The Lord promises to give until the addressee is pleased, joining divine giving to the same future رضى that closes surah 92.
The oath by the day when it discloses brightness closely repeats the section's day opening what the covering night hid.
The oath by the night when it covers closely repeats the covering movement from which the section's road scene begins.
The proportioned soul follows the paired night and day, linking cosmic alternation to a creature made fit.
The soul is shown both its corruption and its taqwa, placing the section's divided moral roads within the walker.
Success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, corresponding to the giver whose wealth-giving seeks purification.
Failure belongs to the one who buries the soul, the downward reversal of purification and disclosed light.
The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger, joining hands, regret, and the road missed.
He wishes he had not taken a particular person as an intimate friend, matching the section's remembered companion who nearly caused his fall.
That friend led him away from remembrance after it reached him, explaining how companionship turns a person from the warning-sign.
Blessed is the One in whose hand is dominion and who has power over everything, directly opposing divine possession and support to the king's doomed grasp.
The question asks who holds sovereignty over everything, protecting while none can protect against Him; hand-like ownership and the section's shield meet in one divine prerogative.
The final abode is for those who do not desire exaltation or corruption on earth, drawing the boundary between the sought Most High and Pharaoh's desire to be high.
Pharaoh proclaims the kingdom of Egypt his and points to rivers beneath him, giving the section's holding king a concrete boast of property and elevation.
Pharaoh denies Moses and disobeys, supplying the denial immediately before his turning and boast of supreme lordship.
He turns away and strives, placing the surah's turning act and its morally divergent striving in the same royal figure.
He gathers the people and calls out, providing the public setting for the claim of height in the next ayah.
Pharaoh's fate is declared a lesson for whoever fears, turning the palace and punishment scene into the protective fear urged by the section.
The one who transgresses begins a compact contrast between self-exaltation and the garden road.
Preferring the nearer life makes worldly possession and status the choice opposed to God's ownership of first and last.
Hell is the refuge for that preference, completing the movement from worldly elevation down to fire.
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains desire takes the protective stance opposite Pharaoh and the self-sufficient miser.
The garden becomes that person's refuge, opposing the high garden of restraint and fear to the fire reached by self-exaltation.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own love of food; this identifies the concrete hand and recipients whose purpose is voiced in 76:9.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend in God's way are warned of punishment, identifying the withheld wealth that becomes branding metal in 9:35.
A garden-dweller says he had a companion, establishing the worldly relationship whose mockery and near-ruin the following ayat recall.
He asks the other people of the garden whether they will look down, introducing the deliberate high-to-low gaze realized in 37:55.
The Helpers prefer others even while in need, and protection from the self's avarice marks success, joining generous preference with the shield against grasping.
The people of the garden taste no death beyond the first, and God protects them from Hell, extending the rescued garden-dweller's reflection on death and fire.
That protection is explicitly a bounty from the Lord and the great success, closely paralleling the saved companion's appeal to his Lord's favor.
Those for whom God's best has preceded are kept far from Hell, a direct counterpart to the God-fearing giver being moved to its side rather than entering it.
They do not even hear Hell and remain in what their souls desire, defining the safe distance that separates sign from burning presence.
God guides the human to the path, after which the person is either grateful or ungrateful, a concise version of one guidance producing two responses.
Chains and a blaze are prepared for the ungrateful, turning one branch of the guided path into entry into fire.
The righteous drink from a prepared cup, beginning the garden-side outcome opposed to the blaze in the preceding ayah.
The question identifies the person who denies judgment, beginning a short sequence in which denial becomes refusal of care for the vulnerable.
That denier drives away the orphan, making rejection of the final account visible as a hand that repels rather than gives.
He does not urge feeding the needy, the direct behavioral reverse of those who feed solely for God's face.
After God gives them from His bounty, they become stingy with it and turn away, the exact reversal of the giver who confirms the good and directs his face toward God.
Charity spoiled by reminders, injury, and display is a thin covering of soil swept from a rock by rain, the barren rain-scene against the high garden that doubles its fruit.
A fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its aged owner most needs it, bringing garden, lost provision, and fire together as the vulnerable reverse of enduring giving.
Those who reject God's signs become companions of the left, the opposite side reached after the same two elevated ways are shown.
A fire closed over the rejecters completes the opposite road from freeing and feeding to confinement in flame.
Other faces on that Day are humbled, reversing the radiant faces produced by protected, God-directed striving.
They have labored and exhausted themselves, showing striving whose direction yields weariness rather than the رضى of 88:9.
They enter a scorching fire, the low outcome opposed to the lofty garden of 88:10.
The disbelievers cannot ward the fire from their faces or backs and receive no help, reversing God's shielding of the givers and recalling the branded front and back.
A condemned person must shield his face from the worst punishment, a grim reversal of God shielding those who gave for His face.
Pharaoh tells his chiefs he knows no god for them but himself and orders a tower built so he can ascend, making self-claimed lordship and manufactured height oppose Moses' giving Lord.
Neither wealth nor children avail against God, and their possessors are companions of the fire, directly bounding wealth's ability to save.
The wealth and children of the disbelievers avail nothing against God and they become fuel for fire, joining failed possession to the blaze.
One who turns from the Messenger after guidance is clear and follows another path is left to that choice and burned in Hell, joining turning, divided way, and fire.
The garden speaker asks whether the saved will die again, continuing his amazed recognition that favor has removed him from the companion's fiery outcome.
He excepts only the first death and asks whether punishment is now absent, helping specify the lasting safety supplied by divine favor.
He names this rescue the great attainment, giving the garden-side outcome of the section's divergent striving.
The command that workers should work for such an outcome links the companion scene back to the surah's claim that human striving is diverse.
Garden and silk are the reward for the feeders' patience, completing the outcome of the giving, face-seeking, and divine shielding in 76:8-11.
Broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the day they meet God, continuing the consequence of receiving bounty, withholding it, and turning away.
Spending in God's way is likened to a grain producing seven multiplied ears, another concrete picture of a giving act becoming growth.
Those who spend without reminder or injury have reward and no fear, identifying the conduct whose fertile image follows in 2:265.
Charitable men and women who extend a good loan to God receive multiplication and a noble reward, joining purification-like charity, increase, and divine return.
A garden owner's fruit is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while its trellises lie fallen, a secondary garden-and-collapse scene where possession cannot hold up its owner.
He has no company to help him apart from God and cannot save himself, clarifying the absence of a human hand at the moment wealth and garden fail.
In that collapsed-garden scene, true protection belongs to God and His outcome is best, returning support and final result to the divine owner.
The garden owners command that no poor person enter their harvest, making a withheld share for the needy the moral cause within the garden scene.
They go out confident in their power to withhold, embodying the self-sufficient grasp that the section places on the descending road.
On seeing the ruined garden they admit they have been deprived, reversing the high garden whose giving yields double fruit.
The condemned person amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, giving the section's clutched and enveloping wealth a recognizable human posture.
He supposes his wealth has made him immortal, the illusion exposed when wealth cannot avail at the fall.
He is to be cast into the Crusher, supplying a downward end to the wealth he treated as enduring support.
The Crusher is identified as God's kindled fire, completing the movement from accumulated wealth to being thrown into flame.
That fire rises over hearts, making punishment attach inwardly as the heated treasure attaches to bodies in the section.
The rebuke that people do not honor the orphan gives the first concrete failure behind their claim that wealth itself is honor.
They do not urge feeding the needy, directly reversing the face-seeking feeders whom God shields.
They consume inheritance voraciously, presenting the grasping relationship to wealth that accompanies failed giving.
They love wealth with intense love, the attachment from which the section's miser expects self-sufficiency.
Hell is brought into view on that Day and the human remembers too late, bringing warning-fire and recognition together after the wealth rebukes.
He wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, the regretful opposite of wealth given beforehand for God's face.
The people in Saqar confess that they were not among those who prayed, beginning their account of how the fire corresponds to their former stance.
They confess that they did not feed the needy, connecting entry into the blaze to the direct opposite of the section's unrecompensed feeding.
They confess that they denied the Day of Judgment, joining lack of giving to the denial that elsewhere turns its back on warning.
Their denial continued until certainty came, marking the instant when ignored warning became an entered reality.
God saves those who had taqwa by their attainment so that evil does not touch or grieve them, another explicit realization of taqwa as a shield.
The people of the garden rejoice in what their Lord gave them and in His protection from Hell, joining divine giving, garden joy, and shielding from fire.
Everything perishes except God's face, and judgment and return belong to Him; this gives ultimate duration and ownership to the face sought by the giver.
The face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains, supporting the section's direction of transient wealth toward the enduring divine face.
The Prophet is told not to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening desiring His face; their mutual accounts are not one another's burden.
He is told to remain with those seeking their Lord's face morning and evening and not turn his eyes toward worldly adornment, joining face, turning, and the pull of possessions.
God's hand is over the hands of those who pledge; breaking the pledge harms oneself, while fulfilling it receives a great reward, joining hand, promise, and divine support.
The guilty wear garments of pitch while fire covers their faces, a bodily reversal of wealth worn like a garment and the face opened by divine protection.
